heading: Duty to have fall protection.
title: Fall protection inspection: OSHA requirements (29 CFR 1926.501)
description: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.501 fall protection requirements by paragraph, citation data for FY2022–FY2026, and a printable fall protection inspection checklist.
opening: 29 CFR 1926.501 requires employers to protect employees from falls of 6 feet (1.8 m) or more to a lower level, mostly with guardrail, safety net or personal fall arrest systems (PFAS), and sets rules for holes, roofs, leading edges and falling objects.

topIndustries.title: Foundation, Structure, and Building Exterior Contractors
Electric Power Generation, Transmission and Distribution
Lumber and Other Construction Materials Merchant Wholesalers

enforcementSummary: 1926.501(b)(13), the residential construction paragraph, is the most cited part of the standard in FY2022–FY2026, followed by 1926.501(b)(1), which covers work at an unprotected side or edge, 1926.501(b)(10) on roofing work on low-slope roofs and 1926.501(b)(11) on steep roofs. Yearly citations stayed between 8,286 and 9,189 from FY2022 to FY2025, then fell to 6,503 in FY2026.
requirementsIntro: 1926.501(a)(1) places the duty to provide fall protection systems on employers and requires every system the section calls for to meet the criteria in 1926.502. Paragraph (a) covers these general duties, paragraphs (b)(1) through (b)(15) set the protection for each type of work area, and paragraph (c) covers falling objects.

requirements.heading: What must an employer confirm before anyone works at height?
requirements.intro: Before employees work on a surface, 1926.501(a) requires the employer to determine that the walking/working surface can support them safely and to use only fall protection that meets 1926.502.

items.text: Every fall protection system required by 1926.501 must conform to the criteria in 1926.502.
The employer must determine whether each walking/working surface has the strength and structural integrity to support employees safely, and allow employees to work only on surfaces that have it.

requirements.heading: When must edges, ramps, wall openings and hoist areas be protected?
requirements.intro: Edges, hoist areas, ramps, walkways, wall openings and other elevated surfaces must be protected once the potential fall reaches the 6-foot height set in 1926.501(b)(1), (b)(3), (b)(6), (b)(14) and (b)(15), with an extra condition for wall openings.

items.text: An employee on a horizontal or vertical walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge 6 feet or more above a lower level needs a guardrail system, safety net system or PFAS.

In a hoist area, employees exposed to a fall of at least 6 feet need guardrails or a PFAS; if a guardrail, chain or gate is removed for hoisting and an employee must lean through or out over the access opening, that employee needs a PFAS.
Ramps, runways and other walkways need guardrail systems where an employee could fall 6 feet or further.

Employees working on, at, above or near a wall opening, including one with a chute attached, need guardrails, safety nets or a PFAS where the outside bottom edge is 6 feet or more above lower levels and the inside bottom edge is less than 39 inches (1.0 m) above the walking/working surface.
Any other walking/working surface at least 6 feet above a lower level needs a guardrail, a net or a PFAS, except where 1926.500(a)(2) or paragraphs (b)(1) through (b)(14) apply.

requirements.heading: How must holes, excavations and dangerous equipment be guarded?
requirements.intro: Holes, excavation edges and dangerous equipment are covered by 1926.501(b)(4), (b)(7) and (b)(8), which name covers, guardrails, fences, barricades, equipment guards or fall arrest depending on the hazard and its depth or height.

items.text: Where a hole, including a skylight, is more than 6 feet above lower levels, employees must be protected from falling through it by a PFAS, a cover or guardrails erected around the hole.
Covers must protect employees from tripping in, or stepping into or through, holes and skylights.
Covers must also protect employees from objects falling through holes and skylights.
At the edge of an excavation 6 feet or deeper that is not readily seen because of plant growth or another visual barrier, employees need guardrail systems, fences or barricades.
At the edge of a well, pit, shaft or similar excavation 6 feet or deeper, employees need guardrail systems, fences, barricades or covers.
An employee less than 6 feet above dangerous equipment must be protected from falling into or onto it by guardrail systems or equipment guards.
An employee 6 feet or higher above dangerous equipment needs guardrail systems, a PFAS or safety net systems.

requirements.heading: What fall protection does roofing work need?
requirements.intro: Roofing work is covered by 1926.501(b)(10) for low-slope roofs, which allows warning line combinations and, on roofs 50 feet or less in width, a safety monitoring system alone, and by 1926.501(b)(11) for steep roofs, which requires guardrails with toeboards, safety nets or a PFAS.

items.text: Except as otherwise provided in paragraph (b), employees doing roofing work on low-slope roofs with unprotected sides and edges 6 feet or higher above lower levels need guardrails, safety nets, a PFAS, or a warning line system combined with a guardrail, safety net, PFAS or safety monitoring system.
On low-slope roofs 50 feet (15.25 m) or less in width, a safety monitoring system may be used alone, without a warning line system (see appendix A to subpart M).
Employees on a steep roof whose unprotected sides and edges are 6 or more feet above lower levels need guardrail systems with toeboards, safety net systems or a PFAS.

requirements.heading: When can a fall protection plan replace guardrails, nets or arrest systems?
requirements.intro: For leading edge work, precast concrete erection and residential construction, 1926.501(b)(2)(i), (b)(12) and (b)(13) allow a fall protection plan meeting 1926.502(k) only when the employer can demonstrate that guardrail, safety net and personal fall arrest systems are infeasible or that they create a greater hazard.

items.text: Each employee constructing a leading edge 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above lower levels needs a guardrail, safety net or personal fall arrest system; if the employer can demonstrate these cannot feasibly be used or would create a greater hazard, it must develop and implement a fall protection plan meeting 1926.502(k).

The standard presumes at least one of those systems is feasible and will not create a greater hazard, so the employer carries the burden of showing that a 1926.502(k) plan is appropriate for the particular workplace situation.

Employees on a surface where leading edges are under construction, but who are not doing that work, need guardrails, nets or a PFAS for falls of 6 feet and above; if guardrails are chosen and a controlled access zone already exists for the leading edge work, a control line may be used instead of a guardrail along the edge parallel to the leading edge.

Employees erecting precast concrete members, such as wall panels, columns, beams and floor and roof tees, or doing related operations such as grouting, at 6 feet and above lower levels need guardrails, safety nets or PFAS unless another provision of paragraph (b) provides an alternative; the same infeasibility exception and plan requirement apply.

Employees in residential construction activities 6 or more feet above lower levels need a guardrail system, safety net system or PFAS unless another paragraph (b) provision allows an alternative measure; where the employer shows those systems would be infeasible or more hazardous, a 1926.502(k) plan applies instead.

requirements.heading: What protection applies to formwork, rebar and overhand bricklaying?
requirements.intro: Formwork, reinforcing steel and overhand bricklaying have their own lists of permitted measures in 1926.501(b)(5) and (b)(9), including positioning device systems for formwork and controlled access zones for bricklaying.

items.text: An employee on the face of formwork or reinforcing steel needs a PFAS, safety net system or positioning device system against falls to lower levels of 6 feet or greater.

Except as otherwise provided in paragraph (b), employees doing overhand bricklaying and related work 6 feet or greater above lower levels need a guardrail system, net or PFAS, or must work in a controlled access zone.
An employee reaching more than 10 inches (25 cm) below the level of the surface they are working on needs a PFAS, safety net or guardrail system.

requirements.heading: How must employees be protected from falling objects?
requirements.intro: When an employee is exposed to falling objects, 1926.501(c) requires the employer to have each employee wear a hard hat and to implement one of the measures in 1926.501(c)(1) to (c)(3).

items.text: Each employee exposed to falling objects must wear a hard hat.
Erect toeboards, screens or guardrail systems so objects cannot fall from higher levels.
Erect a canopy structure and keep potential falling objects far enough from the edge of the higher level that they would not go over if accidentally displaced.
Barricade the area where objects could fall, prohibit employees from entering it, and keep objects far enough from the edge that they would not go over if accidentally displaced.

checklistIntro: This checklist covers each protection duty in 1926.501(a), (b) and (c) for supervisors checking work at height and the areas below it where objects could fall.

faq.question: Does 1926.501 cover bricklaying done from scaffolds?
faq.answer: The note to 1926.501(b)(9)(ii) says bricklaying operations performed on scaffolds are regulated by subpart L (Scaffolds) of Part 1926, so check that subpart for scaffold work.
